name: rhabdoid tumour
aliases: malignant rhabdoid tumour of the kidney

reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours: Paediatric Tumours
clinicalPearls: A highly aggressive malignancy of infancy and early childhood; the kidney is the prototypical site (malignant rhabdoid tumour of the kidney), but soft tissue, liver, and other viscera are also affected.
Defined by biallelic inactivation of SMARCB1 (INI1/hSNF5) on chromosome 22q11.2, with a small subset driven by SMARCA4 (BRG1) loss.
Loss of nuclear INI1 (SMARCB1) expression on immunohistochemistry is the diagnostic hallmark and distinguishes it from mimics such as Wilms tumour.
A substantial minority arise within rhabdoid tumour predisposition syndrome from a germline SMARCB1 or SMARCA4 mutation, so germline testing and genetic counselling are essential.
Synchronous or metachronous central nervous system atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumour occurs, making brain imaging mandatory at staging.
Hypercalcaemia is a recognised paraneoplastic feature of renal rhabdoid tumour.
Presentation is often with a rapidly growing abdominal or flank mass, haematuria, and systemic upset in a very young infant.
Metastatic disease at diagnosis is common and the prognosis is among the worst of paediatric solid tumours.
reference.pathophysiology: Rhabdoid tumours are driven by loss of function of the SWI/SNF (BAF) chromatin-remodelling complex, most often through biallelic inactivation of SMARCB1 (INI1) and less commonly SMARCA4 (BRG1). Loss of a core subunit deregulates chromatin accessibility and enhancer activity, impairing differentiation and driving proliferation despite an otherwise remarkably stable, near-diploid genome with few additional mutations. Tumours are composed of characteristic rhabdoid cells with eccentric nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and eosinophilic cytoplasmic hyaline inclusions corresponding to whorls of intermediate filaments. A germline SMARCB1 or SMARCA4 alteration (rhabdoid tumour predisposition syndrome) predisposes to multifocal, very early-onset disease, including concurrent central nervous system tumours.
additionalDifferentials: Clear cell sarcoma of the kidney
Atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumour when the central nervous system is involved
Epithelioid sarcoma (also INI1-deficient) at soft-tissue sites
Renal medullary carcinoma (also SMARCB1-deficient) in older children
additionalInvestigations: SMARCB1/INI1 (and SMARCA4) immunohistochemistry on tumour tissue
Molecular and cytogenetic testing for SMARCB1 deletion or mutation
Germline SMARCB1/SMARCA4 testing and genetic counselling
Brain and whole-spine MRI to exclude synchronous central nervous system rhabdoid tumour
Cross-sectional imaging of chest, abdomen, and pelvis for staging
Serum calcium to detect paraneoplastic hypercalcaemia
redFlags: Neurological signs or a brain lesion indicating synchronous atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumour
A rapidly enlarging mass with systemic deterioration in an infant
reference.prognosis: Extracranial rhabdoid tumour carries a poor prognosis, particularly in infants and in those with metastatic disease or a germline predisposition. Intensified multimodal therapy achieves long-term survival in only a minority.
pitfalls: Misclassifying the tumour as Wilms tumour or another blastemal-rich neoplasm without performing INI1 immunohistochemistry.
Omitting brain imaging and thereby missing a synchronous central nervous system rhabdoid tumour.
Failing to arrange germline SMARCB1/SMARCA4 testing, missing predisposition syndrome and family risk.
Attributing hypercalcaemia to another cause and overlooking a paraneoplastic mechanism.
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Paediatric Tumours
management: Treat with intensive multimodal therapy combining multi-agent chemotherapy, surgical resection and radiotherapy for local control
Stage with brain and whole-spine imaging to detect synchronous atypical teratoid or rhabdoid central nervous system tumour
Undertake germline SMARCB1 and SMARCA4 testing with genetic counselling for rhabdoid tumour predisposition syndrome
Detect and manage paraneoplastic hypercalcaemia with hydration and appropriate hypocalcaemic agents
Enrol in clinical trials and consider novel targeted agents such as EZH2 inhibitors given poor outcomes with standard therapy
Provide multidisciplinary paediatric oncology care with supportive and, where appropriate, palliative input
